```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 11,
                      fig.height = 4.4, dpi = 110, out.width = "100%")
library(psychnets)
has_cograph <- requireNamespace("cograph", quietly = TRUE)
```

## What the model estimates

Panel data measure the same people a few times. The panel graphical
vector-autoregressive model (panel-GVAR; Epskamp, 2020) splits each person's
scores into a stable personal level and week-to-week deviations from it, and
estimates three networks:

* a **temporal** network: does being above one's own level on one variable in
  one wave predict the next wave? Arrows are lag-1 effects; self-loops are
  autoregressive (carry-over) effects.
* a **contemporaneous** network: which deviations move together within a wave,
  after the lagged effects (partial correlations)?
* a **between-person** network: how are the stable personal levels related
  (partial correlations)?

`panel_gvar()` fits the model of `psychonetrics::panelgvar()` by maximum
likelihood, entirely in base R, and certifies the optimum.

## The data

`srl_panel` is a synthetic panel of 100 students measured in four consecutive
weeks on five self-regulated-learning indicators (0-100 scales). It was
simulated from a panel-GVAR whose structure was taken from real
experience-sampling data, so it is realistic and fully shareable (see
`?srl_panel`). The data are in long format: one row per student per week.

```{r data}
head(srl_panel)
vars <- c("efficacy", "planning", "effort", "enjoyment", "anxiety")
```

## The full model

By default every edge is estimated and reported with its standard error and
p-value; nothing is removed.

```{r full}
fit <- panel_gvar(srl_panel, vars = vars, id = "student", wave = "week")
fit
```

The edge table has one row per edge, with a 95% Wald interval and a
`significant` flag at `alpha = 0.01`:

```{r full-edges}
head(as.data.frame(fit), 8)
summary(fit)
```

`plot()` draws the three networks on one layout. **Solid edges are
significant, dashed edges are not**; blue is positive, vermillion negative, and
the weight is printed on each edge.

```{r plot-full, eval = has_cograph}
plot(fit)
```

```{r full-numbers, include = FALSE}
edges <- as.data.frame(fit)
ar <- subset(edges, network == "temporal" & from == to & significant)
cross <- subset(edges, network == "temporal" & from != to & significant)
contemporaneous <- subset(edges, network == "contemporaneous" & significant)
between <- subset(edges, network == "between" & significant)
show <- function(d, sep) paste(sprintf("%s%s%s (%.2f)", d$from, sep, d$to,
                                       d$weight), collapse = ", ")
```

Reading the significant edges:

* **Temporal.** `r nrow(ar)` of the 5 autoregressive effects are
  significant (`r show(ar, " -> ")`): a student who is above their own level in
  one week tends to stay above it the next. One lagged effect between
  variables is significant: `r show(cross, " -> ")`.
* **Contemporaneous.** `r nrow(contemporaneous)` edges
  (`r show(contemporaneous, "-")`): in weeks when a student's efficacy,
  planning, effort and enjoyment are above their usual level, they rise
  together. Anxiety is not connected.
* **Between-person.** `r nrow(between)` edges (`r show(between, "-")`):
  `r paste(sprintf("students with a higher personal level of %s tend to have a %s personal level of %s", between$from, ifelse(between$weight > 0, "higher", "lower"), between$to), collapse = "; ")`.
  Between-person edges are estimated from only 100 personal levels, so they
  carry more uncertainty than the within-person ones.

## Selecting edges

Marking significance does not change the model. To report a sparser network,
`panel_gvar()` offers two selection methods.

`select = "prune"` removes every edge with p > 0.01 in one pass, refits, and
then runs a **step-up** search that adds edges back while they significantly
improve the model and lower BIC (psychonetrics' `prune()` followed by
`stepup()`). The step-up matters: edges that stand in for each other, such as
an autoregression and a correlated lagged effect, can each look unnecessary
while the other is present, and one-pass pruning would remove both.

```{r prune}
pruned <- panel_gvar(srl_panel, vars = vars, id = "student", wave = "week",
                     select = "prune")
pruned
```

The pruned model keeps 4 autoregressive effects, 2 lagged effects between
variables, 5 contemporaneous and 4 between-person edges. The step-up search
re-added 3 of the edges that one-pass pruning had removed, and the sparser model
still fits acceptably (CFI = 0.969, RMSEA = 0.037).

```{r plot-prune, eval = has_cograph}
plot(pruned)
```

`select = "ebic"` instead shrinks edges with a lasso penalty chosen by EBIC --
the panel counterpart of `ebic_glasso()` (psychonetrics'
`panelgvar(estimator = "PML")`). Weak edges become exactly zero in one
optimization. The estimates are penalized, so they carry no p-values
(`refit = TRUE` refits the selected network without the penalty). A shorter
penalty path keeps this example fast:

```{r ebic}
lasso <- panel_gvar(srl_panel, vars = vars, id = "student", wave = "week",
                    select = "ebic", nlambda = 20)
summary(lasso)
```

```{r ebic-numbers, include = FALSE}
lasso_between <- subset(summary(lasso), network == "between")$edges
```

The lasso keeps the temporal and contemporaneous structure but
`r if (lasso_between == 0) "no between-person edge" else paste(lasso_between, "between-person edges")`:
with 100 students the penalty is more conservative than the significance-based
selection for the between-person network.

## When wave means drift

The model assumes **stationary means**: the average level of each variable does
not change across waves. If it drifts (for instance a steady decline across a
term), `standardize = "z_per_wave"` z-scores every variable within every wave,
which removes the drift; the edges are then standardized.

```{r standardize}
z_fit <- panel_gvar(srl_panel, vars = vars, id = "student", wave = "week",
                    standardize = "z_per_wave")
subset(as.data.frame(z_fit, what = "fit"), select = c(chisq, df, cfi, rmsea))
```

## Fit and diagnostics

Fit indices compare the model with the saturated model and with a baseline
without temporal or network structure:

```{r fit-indices}
as.data.frame(fit, what = "fit")
```

The diagnostics report the optimality certificate (the largest remaining
gradient of the likelihood, ~0 at the optimum), whether any part of the
solution sits on a boundary of the parameter space, whether standard errors
exist, and how many of the three optimizer starts reached the best optimum:

```{r diagnostics}
as.data.frame(fit, what = "diagnostics")
```

The variance split shows how much of each variable is stable between students
and how much fluctuates within them:

```{r variance}
as.data.frame(fit, what = "variance")
```

## Reference

Epskamp, S. (2020). Psychometric network models from time-series and panel
data. *Psychometrika*, 85(1), 206-231.
[doi:10.1007/s11336-020-09697-3](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-020-09697-3)
